books.title: Preeti Karan Setu Banhal
books.subtitle: A Bridge Built for the Sake of Love · Redefining Maithili
books.description: Picture narrative, literary form, public libraries and the work of preservation.
books.editionNote: The title page uses Ashish Anchinhar; signed contributions use Ashish Anchinhaar. No English translator credit or publication year was identified in the supplied front matter.

books.title: Setusham: Vibrant Maithili
books.subtitle: Second volume · title page: Setushama: Vibrant Maithili
books.description: Digital language, new writers, diversity and the responsibilities of a literary public.
books.editionNote: The title page spells the title Setushama; the running title uses Setusham. It credits translation from Maithili into English to Gajendra Thakur. No publication year was identified in the supplied front matter.

articles.title: First, the verse to Ganesha was sung… — Editorial
articles.author: Ashish Anchinhaar
articles.gist: Anchinhaar explains the volume’s three sections, its mixture of older and newly commissioned writing, and its folk-song framework. He asks readers to recognize Nagendra Kumar Jha and Panjikar Vidyanand Jha in jointly edited work, even where articles omit them. He identifies subjects still awaiting assessment and invites corrections. His account of editorial vision, spelling variation and linked references clarifies how this particular collection was assembled.

articles.title: Presentation: specialties and contributions
articles.author: Ashish Anchinhaar
articles.gist: This numbered presentation assembles the editor’s account of Preeti’s picture stories and Gajendra’s digital, archival, linguistic and publishing work. It distinguishes transliteration technology from expertise in every script and describes Wikipedia as collaborative. Drawn from Anchinhaar’s history of web journalism, the list repeatedly makes priority claims but also invites documented corrections. It is an editorial reference framework, not a separately verified chronology.

articles.title: Turning the Pages, the Village’s Director: K.N.T.
articles.author: Siyaram Jha ‘Saras’
articles.gist: Saras remembers Kripanand Thakur through the institutions of village life: tutoring, the Rambahadur public library, theatre, football and engineering service. Personal recollections show how collective effort widened educational and cultural opportunities, and how factional conflict could undo them. The concluding account of professional integrity connects this remembered example with Gajendra and Preeti’s work. It is a participant’s biographical memoir, not an independently verified institutional history.
articles.note: The contents give a different English rendering: “The Village Director Who Turned the Crank: K.N.T.” Reprinted from Videha, issue 386, 15 January 2024, according to p. 79.

articles.title: Preeti Thakur’s Gonu Jha and Other Maithili Picture Stories
articles.author: Dr. Shefalika Verma
articles.gist: Verma connects her appreciation of Preeti Thakur’s picture stories with a wider concern about women’s exclusion from literary criticism. She values the book’s compression of remembered folk narratives into an accessible visual form and suggests extending this work to legends of the Kosi. The piece is an appreciative response and a proposal for future storytelling.

articles.title: Gonu Jha and Other Maithili Picture Stories
articles.author: Prof. Veena Thakur
articles.gist: Thakur reads the interplay of words, lines and colour as a means of transmitting Mithila’s folk culture. Moving through the collection’s heroes and traditions, she argues that picture narrative expands Mithila painting beyond familiar ceremonial subjects. Her discussion links artistic change with cultural continuity and emphasizes women’s role in preserving and renewing folk art.

articles.title: Gonu Jha Aan Maithili Chitrakatha and Maithili Chitrakatha
articles.author: Dr. Raman Jha
articles.gist: Jha places the two collections beside oral storytelling and the weakening use of Maithili with children. He stresses how words and pictures share narrative work, enabling familiar folk figures to become visible to young readers. His praise rests on accessible language and intergenerational transmission; an editorial note records the article’s later inclusion in his Parijat Manjari.

articles.title: Gonu Jha and Other Maithili Picture Stories
articles.author: Shiv Kumar Jha ‘Tillu’
articles.gist: Jha examines individual tales, their appeal to children and their representation of Mithila across caste and regional boundaries. He distinguishes the imaginative force of legend from historical verification, praises the simple language and visual presentation, and notes a specific weakness in the lion illustration. The review combines cultural appreciation with observations about how the pictures work.

articles.title: A Look at Preeti Thakur’s Both Picture Story Books
articles.author: Dharendra Kumar
articles.gist: Kumar treats the two picture-story collections as a way of preserving narratives previously held in communal memory. He compares visual storytelling with the supplementary work of colour, sound and light in theatre, and emphasizes that images can communicate even before children recognize letters. His central concern is the enrichment of an underdeveloped area of Maithili publishing.
articles.note: The contents gives ‘Dhirendra Kumar’; the article heading prints ‘Dharendra Kumar’.

articles.title: Beautiful Picture Stories for Children
articles.author: Durganand Mandal
articles.gist: Mandal recalls courtyard storytelling and follows the collections through love stories, folk heroes and community traditions. He particularly values their breadth of caste representation and their recovery of narratives for children accustomed to magazines in other languages. His argument presents the books as entertaining cultural preservation; historical and priority assertions remain the contributor’s claims.

articles.title: Maithili Picture Story
articles.author: Shiv Kumar Jha ‘Tillu’
articles.gist: Jha asks what constitutional recognition means if children cease speaking Maithili. He sees the collection’s strongest contribution in its inclusion of stories from different communities and regions, including Begusarai and Musahar traditions. He distinguishes the retelling of inherited tales from inventing new plots, while praising the editing, illustrations and capacity to encourage attachment to the language.

articles.title: Folk Deities of Mithila
articles.author: Shiv Kumar Jha ‘Tillu’
articles.gist: Jha evaluates the book through children’s needs, migration and the transmission of festivals and folk memory. He argues that inherited plots can still acquire value through new illustrations and participatory colouring pages. Alongside praise for the visual treatment, he finds some narrative transitions too compressed and asks for fuller storytelling, particularly where one tale shifts abruptly into another.

articles.title: The Early History of Maithili Picture Story (2002 to 2016)
articles.author: Ashish Anchinhaar
articles.gist: Anchinhaar constructs a chronology that separates translated picture books, original collections and magazine publication. He situates Preeti Thakur’s early translations and later originals alongside the work of other creators and the spread of web publishing. His account challenges an existing priority claim while explicitly inviting evidence of earlier examples; its publication-history assertions are presented as his research position.

articles.title: Interview with Preeti Thakur
articles.author: Preeti Thakur; interviewed by Ashish Anchinhaar
articles.gist: Thakur recalls childhood reading and drawing, explains her interest in making Maithili picture books, and stresses language and pictures that children enjoy. She discusses print and digital reading, her preference for staying away from public platforms, and the practical division of work at home: her husband sometimes contributes ideas and helps with lettering, while she makes the pictures.

articles.title: Videha Digital Library: A Boon for People Fond of Reading and Studying
articles.author: Kalpana Jha
articles.gist: Kalpana Jha approaches the digital library through readers’ practical difficulties: obtaining books, finding space, paying for them and locating material suited to their interests. She values free access to rare literature, research and examination resources. Her appreciation includes concrete repairs: broken links, disordered pages and the need for alphabetical arrangements of titles and authors. Accessibility here means a collection that can actually be navigated and read.

articles.title: The Founder of Maithili Digital Journalism: Gajendra Thakur
articles.author: Kirtinath Jha
articles.gist: Kirtinath Jha considers money, distribution and editorial acceptance as barriers to Maithili publication. He presents Videha’s regular digital publication and free archive as responses that give new writers and geographically dispersed readers greater access. He also acknowledges limitations in the early material and continuing limits to diversity. Special issues and examination resources exemplify the platform’s range; his conclusion is appreciative without treating its development as complete.
articles.note: The contents use “Pioneer” where the article heading uses “Founder”.

articles.title: The Internet Man of Maithili: Gajendra Thakur
articles.author: Lal Dev Kamat
articles.gist: Kamat places Gajendra Thakur’s work within the transition from print to electronic communication. His central concern is how credit for collaborative language projects is recorded: he distinguishes preparatory Wikipedia work from later approval and points readers towards documentary correspondence. The essay links this argument to early websites and multiscript publication. Its priority claims and account of disputed credit remain the contributor’s claims, rather than independently established conclusions.

articles.title: Gajendra Thakur’s Contribution to Panji Literature
articles.author: Binayanand Jha
articles.gist: Jha welcomes the jointly edited Panji volumes while testing their genealogical readings against other records. Comparisons of Mandar lineages expose variant names, missing generations and uncertain identifications; a proposed reconciliation remains provisional. He asks for better indexes of ancestral villages and branches and further research on royal genealogies. The essay demonstrates why making manuscripts available and establishing a reliable lineage are different scholarly tasks.
articles.note: The heading spells the author Binayanand; the contents use Binyanand. An editorial response on pp. 170–171 discusses separate publication and attribution disputes; it is not the contributor’s conclusion.

articles.title: What is Panji Prabandh?
articles.author: Jagdish Chandra Thakur ‘Anil’
articles.gist: Anil introduces Panji terminology, record types, genealogists and the relationship between marriage documentation and social hierarchy. He emphasizes the difficulty posed by unfamiliar scripts and the value of transliteration for readers. Crucially, he says that many pages remain unread: this is an introductory response during an unfinished reading, not a comprehensive assessment. The historical rules described in the essay should be distinguished from present-day endorsement of them.

articles.title: Dushan Panji: Gajendra Thakur’s Universal Contribution to Maithili Culture
articles.author: Dr. Kailash Kumar Mishra
articles.gist: Mishra reads Panji as a record of social arrangements whose exclusions require examination. Dushan records, including accounts of marriages outside prescribed boundaries, complicate idealized narratives of purity. He proposes comparing manuscripts and transcriptions, training readers in Tirhuta and extending attention to women and other communities. The long discussion is a sociological research agenda as much as a book response; he cautions against excessive scientific claims and acknowledges limits to his assessment.

articles.title: Panji of Mithila and Shri Gajendra Thakur’s Efforts towards its Preservation
articles.author: Bhavanath Jha
articles.gist: Bhavanath Jha distinguishes genealogical records from prescriptive marriage rules and values the broad preservation of fragile material, including incidental documents. He nevertheless treats the available collection as partial. Missing headings, inconsistent visual hierarchy, disordered leaves and unwieldy files impede research; he recommends clearer organization and improved scans. The essay insists that preservation must be followed by editorial work that makes documents intelligible and findable.
articles.note: The contents spell the author Bhavnath.

articles.title: Courtesy-Murti Shri Gajendra Babu
articles.author: Bhimnath Jha
articles.gist: Bhimnath Jha’s personal tribute centers on the circulation of books and attentive collaboration. He recalls taking the Braille edition of Sahasrabadhanee to a school for blind pupils, sharing books with institutions and discussing genealogy by telephone. His example of including daughters in a family record makes recognition concrete. Hospitality and practical acts of access, rather than a systematic literary judgment, give the memoir its substance.
articles.note: The contents spell the author Bhimanath. An editorial note at the end adds institutional context about the Braille edition.

articles.title: Gajendra Thakur: Preserver of Mithila’s Heritage
articles.author: Dr. Shiv Kumar Mishra
articles.gist: Mishra sets manuscript digitization against the practical difficulties of conservation: reluctant owners, limited cooperation and the declining ability to read older scripts. His account of a conservation initiative stresses the trust needed to work with custodians. He values Gajendra Thakur’s preservation work while calling for script training and sustained scholarly attention. A preserved image alone cannot ensure that a manuscript’s contents remain accessible to future readers.

articles.title: On Gajendra Thakur’s Maithili-English, English-Maithili, and English-Maithili Computer Dictionaries
articles.author: Uday Narayan Singh ‘Nachiketa’
articles.gist: Singh situates the dictionaries within lexicographic practice and the changing needs of Maithili speakers. Questions of audience, entry selection, pronunciation, regional vocabulary and technical terminology matter more than simply accumulating words. His discussion connects usable reference design with multilingual life and contemporary knowledge. The dictionaries emerge as tools that require explicit editorial choices and continuing development, with the joint contributors’ labor acknowledged.
articles.note: The article records an earlier Videha WordPress publication dated 19 July 2009. Joint dictionary work includes Nagendra Kumar Jha and Panjikar Vidyanand Jha.

articles.title: Shri Gajendra Thakur: In My View
articles.author: Pranav Kumar Jha
articles.gist: Pranav Kumar Jha recalls discovering Maithili resources through a college computer laboratory and later receiving encouragement for his own writing. Free books, examination material and approachable editorial contact made participation possible without extensive formal study of Maithili. He also values children’s resources that connect Maithili directly with English. The account is grounded in a reader-writer’s experience; it does not claim personal intimacy or measured examination outcomes.

articles.title: Mithila Mihir and Videha Web Magazine
articles.author: Lakshman Jha ‘Sagar’
articles.gist: Sagar compares two publishing environments: Mithila Mihir’s print readership and literary formation, and Videha’s digital circulation, regularity and broader admission of writers. He emphasizes living-writer special issues, flexible spelling and access across distance. Personal exchanges and gifts of books support his appreciation of Gajendra and Preeti. The comparison is a participant’s historical perspective; inconsistent elapsed-year statements in the supplied text are not used to establish a chronology.
articles.note: The contents spell the author Laxman.

articles.title: Special Issues in Maithili Magazines (Special Reference—Person Centric Special Issues)
articles.author: Shivshankar Srinivas
articles.gist: Srinivas surveys author-centered magazine issues and argues that evaluation during a writer’s lifetime can encourage further work. He distinguishes their potential critical independence from celebratory volumes and explicitly limits the survey to his knowledge. An appended editorial explanation describes Videha’s selection process and the Nit Naval series, acknowledging that limited resources can leave deserving writers unselected. The survey and the editor’s institutional explanation are separate voices.
articles.note: The editor says he changed the original title “Patrika Visheshank”. The contents use “Theme-Based”; the heading specifies person-centric issues. Editorial material begins on p. 299.

articles.title: Shri Gajendra Thakur ji’s Invaluable Contribution for Maithili: Videha e-Journal
articles.author: Rabindra Narayan Mishra
articles.gist: Mishra describes how editorial support became a practical writing skill: software supplied after a handwritten submission helped him learn to compose and correct work digitally, alongside Umesh Mandal’s assistance. He records the serial publication of his works and values the archive’s usefulness to readers and students. His comparison with the loss of Mithila Mihir centers on continuity, ease of publication and the encouragement of new writers.

articles.title: Videha and Gajendra
articles.author: Dhanakar Thakur
articles.gist: Dhanakar Thakur appreciates regular publication and a useful archive while resisting an identification of the journal with one individual. He questions extensive plot disclosure, parallel awards, insufficient chronological organization of portraits and the balance of institution-focused coverage. He also acknowledges that he has not read Videha thoroughly. This is a qualified endorsement with specific disagreements, followed by an editorial note directing readers to Videha’s response on criticism.
articles.note: The editorial note occupies pp. 313–314 and is distinct from Thakur’s contribution.

articles.title: Maithili Literature’s Seeker-Worshipper Shri Gajendra Thakur
articles.author: Dr. Yoganand Jha
articles.gist: Yoganand Jha links literary creation with the recovery of endangered vocabulary, oral narratives and neglected writing. His main example is Gajendra Thakur’s work on devotional poet Ramji Chaudhary: publication and interpretation allow an overlooked corpus to re-enter circulation. Discussions of Shit-Basant and older words extend the argument. He presents research, republication and the digital archive as connected forms of preservation that can guide future scholars.

articles.title: Gajendra Thakur’s Kurukshetram Antarmanak
articles.author: Uday Narayan Singh ‘Nachiketa’
articles.gist: Singh reads the seven-part collection as an experiment in bringing research, fiction, poetry, drama and children’s writing together under one author. He notices cultural range, political commentary and a creative voice distinct from the lexicographer’s technical persona. The book can be approached as a meta-text or a modern epic, but his praise is qualified: he finds uneven quality across its abundant material.
articles.note: The source records publication on Videha’s WordPress version on 9 June 2009.

articles.title: Gajendra Thakur and His Novel
articles.author: Ashok
articles.gist: Ashok contrasts the two novels Sahasrabadhanee and Sahasrashirsha. The first examines honesty and corruption through successive generations and government service; the second gathers village histories, songs, caste narratives and local knowledge into an expansive social landscape. He values the latter’s recording of oral history and the former’s attention to institutional workings. A preliminary account of digital activity frames, but does not replace, the discussion of fiction.

articles.title: Sahastrabadhanee: In My View (Some Comments)
articles.author: Arvind Thakur
articles.gist: Arvind Thakur examines four generations, documentary detail, memory and the novel’s movement beyond a narrowly regional literary frame. He values coherence and readability, yet argues that corruption’s wider public consequences receive too little development compared with personal loss. Having read the English and Maithili versions, he prefers the English reading. His concluding uncertainty over the comet’s symbolism leaves a genuine interpretive question open rather than resolving it through praise.

articles.title: A Letter for Kurukshetram Antarmanak (A Review in Epistolary Style)
articles.author: Rajdeo Mandal
articles.gist: Writing as an engaged reader rather than claiming professional critical authority, Mandal moves through the collection’s genres. He appreciates the recovery of folk narratives, concise dramatic dialogue, stories of inequality, the novel’s everyday language and the curiosity of children’s poetry. Individual examples make his response more than a general tribute. He also notes difficulty with an epic title while welcoming the opportunity for different readers to find different kinds of writing together.
articles.note: The source records publication on the Videha-operated Maithili Samalochna blog on 7 April 2012.

articles.title: Kurukshetram Antarmanak
articles.author: Shiv Kumar Jha ‘Tillu’
articles.gist: Tillu’s extended review welcomes the collection’s social reach and especially its children’s section, while making unevenness visible. He questions some borrowed English words, the artistry or emotional force of several stories and Sankarshan’s suitability for staging. He finds technical website material beyond his understanding and identifies missing places in the regional survey. Later references to expanded stories complicate the article’s dating; its praise should not erase these concrete reservations.
articles.note: The closing credit says 7 April 2012, but the supplied text also discusses 2023 publications and later Videha issues. It is cited here as the supplied version, not an unchanged 2012 text.

articles.title: Maithili Children’s Poetry Stream
articles.author: Professor Premshankar Singh
articles.gist: Singh examines children’s poems through curiosity, family affection, school, holidays, play and the unequal circumstances of childhood. His examples place delight alongside hunger and child labor. He values a flexible vocabulary that accommodates everyday international words without losing rural Maithili expression. The essay’s account of child psychology is a literary interpretation supported by selected poems, rather than an empirical study of young readers.
articles.note: Reprinted from Videha, issue 70, 15 November 2010, according to the closing credit.

articles.title: Story Penetrating to the Layer of Social Inequality
articles.author: Abha Jha
articles.gist: Abha Jha reads Parvat Upar Bhamara Je Sutal through property, widowhood, caste, migration, disability and institutional injustice. Contrasts with Premchand and discussion of individual stories identify different ways of exposing social relations. Her praise of intellectual range remains qualified: dense reasoning and classical references can obstruct narrative interest and flow. She treats the English self-translations as an attempt to reach beyond Maithili readers, without making that outreach the sole measure of the work.

articles.title: Litterateur Gajendra Thakur: Personality and Work
articles.author: Acharya Ramanand Mandal
articles.gist: Mandal presents Gajendra Thakur’s criticism, biographies and publishing work as support for writers marginalized by dominant literary institutions. He names a broad parallel corpus and connects recognition with access to education and archives. The appended editor explicitly disputes the essay’s equation of ideology with caste identity, explaining Videha’s distinction between caste and mindset. That disagreement is essential to the contribution’s reception, not a detail to smooth away.
articles.note: The editorial response on p. 435 is separate from Mandal’s article. Historical and numerical assertions in the profile are not independently verified here.

articles.title: Maithili’s True Servant: Mr. Gajendra Thakur Ji
articles.author: Ajit Kumar Jha
articles.gist: Drawing on magazine distribution, Ajit Kumar Jha argues that readers’ difficulty obtaining suitable books cannot be solved by celebrating writers alone. He welcomes free digital access but recognizes authors’ interest in royalties and proposes paid electronic distribution too. An editorial response describes earlier Kindle experiments and language-labeling difficulties. The result is a discussion of readership, preservation and sustainable circulation, with the contributor’s proposal distinguished from the editor’s account.
articles.note: The Kindle discussion describes the circumstances reported in this edition; it is not current platform guidance. Editorial response: pp. 443–444.

articles.title: Gajendra Thakur, Giving a New Dimension to Maithili Web Journalism
articles.author: Mukesh Dutt
articles.gist: Dutt begins with books received through his father’s magazine-distribution contacts, then surveys the digital and archival work those encounters helped him discover. Panji editions, script support, dictionaries and internet publication form the main outline. The essay is an appreciative introduction drawing readers towards Ashish Anchinhaar’s history of web journalism; its broad priority claims are presented as part of that account rather than independently established milestones.

articles.title: Discussion of Shruti Publication, which brought Panji Management Publication, and Nagendra Kumar Jha
articles.author: Ashish Anchinhaar
articles.gist: Anchinhaar explains Shruti Publication through a model in which authors do not pay for publication and retain copyright. He distinguishes Gajendra Thakur’s creative and editorial role from Nagendra Kumar Jha’s resource and technical support, then discusses Panji publication and opportunities for new writers. A numbered list of 100 titles makes the essay a publishing record as well as an argument about access. Financial figures remain the editor’s reported figures.
articles.note: The contents use a longer variant of the title. The publication list is integral to this article, pp. 453–464; its historical prices are not current offers.

articles.title: A Comprehensive Conversation with Gajendra Thakur
articles.author: Munnaji, interviewer; Gajendra Thakur, respondent
articles.gist: Munnaji asks about literary beginnings, genre, editorial inclusion, publishing resources and recognition. Gajendra Thakur explains research, dictionaries, script work and creative writing as mutually supporting activities, and describes the collected volume as intended for a family readership. He credits collaborators and practical support while defending publication beyond closed literary circles. These are the respondent’s explanations of his practice, including polemical judgments, rather than independent findings about other writers.
articles.note: The supplied heading describes Munnaji as a writer and critic. The closing credit names Purvottar Maithil, January–March 2011, and Videha-Sadeha 33, but updated issue counts appear in the supplied version.

articles.title: Interview of Gajendra Thakur
articles.author: Ashish Anchinhaar, interviewer; Gajendra Thakur, respondent
articles.gist: This email interview revisits the earlier conversation in light of new Panji and internet assessments. Questions address institutions, writing volume, criticism, editorial participation and the parallel literary stream. Thakur resists judging quality by age or quantity and describes consistency across work and life as important. The closing exchange disputes the classification of a literary event; it is an interviewee’s contested account, not an independently adjudicated history.
articles.note: The heading explicitly credits Ashish Anchinhaar with conducting the interview by email.

articles.title: Introduction, bibliography and photograph captions
articles.author: Editorial compilation; no separate byline
articles.gist: This appendix presents biographical context and bibliographies grouped by original writing, translation, script versions, audio resources and joint editorship. It explains why constituent works of a collected volume may receive separate catalogue numbers and credits Preeti’s scanning and cataloguing of the Panji material. Family acknowledgments and photograph captions accompany the lists. The summary preserves the bibliographic function without treating its historical catalogue as a current exhaustive inventory.

articles.title: Closing reflection and contributor introductions
articles.author: Ashish Anchinhaar (editorial material)
articles.gist: The closing folk-song frame imagines the couple’s work continuing into future generations. It then explains the linked contributor names, the limits of those links for print readers, and the possibility of link failure. A brief editor biography completes the volume’s credits. These pages provide editorial closure and a guide to attribution, rather than another critical article.

articles.title: Ganapati invocation — Editorial
articles.author: Ashish Anchinhaar
articles.gist: Anchinhaar explains Setushama’s bridge metaphor through a Samavedic hymn and links it to ethical obstacles in literary life. He describes the second volume as a complement to the first, commissioned mainly from different contributors and composed of new articles. Seven invocations structure its presentation. The preface acknowledges subjects still uncovered and welcomes corrections; its Vedic interpretation and account of the literary field remain the editor’s framing.

articles.title: Rijuneeti no Varuno Mitro… — Presentation of contributions
articles.author: Ashish Anchinhaar
articles.gist: The editor repeats and extends a reference list of Preeti and Gajendra’s contributions so the second volume can be approached without constantly consulting the first. Picture books, Panji access, multiscript publication, dictionaries and collaborative language projects supply its framework. The list draws on Anchinhaar’s history of web journalism and explicitly remains open to correction. Its claims of firstness are not converted here into independently verified facts.

articles.title: A Proficient Writer of the Child’s Mind — Mrs. Preeti Thakur
articles.author: Munni Kamat
articles.gist: Kamat argues that children’s writing requires simplicity of feeling and an imaginative return to the child’s perspective. Surveying four books, she highlights their illustrations and cultural transmission. Her most concrete example is the Purusha Pariksha activity book, where children identify stories, supply titles and dialogue, and colour drawings—combining literary inheritance with active participation.

articles.title: Preeti Thakur’s Contribution to Maithili Picture Stories
articles.author: Ira Mallick
articles.gist: Mallick situates picture narrative between oral storytelling, visual art and children’s first encounters with language. She surveys translations and original collections, praises the use of line, colour and Mithila painting techniques, and emphasizes accessibility before alphabetic literacy. The essay interprets the books as a connection between younger readers and regional culture; its broad claims are attributed to Mallick.

articles.title: The Creator of the Digital Era for Maithili: Gajendra Thakur
articles.author: Kailash Kumar Thakur
articles.gist: Thakur surveys digital publishing, Wikipedia, dictionaries, manuscript access and multiple scripts, then argues that textual resources alone cannot secure Maithili’s future. He proposes podcasts, oral histories, video essays and subtitled scholarly conversations. The appended editorial response welcomes the challenge but points to existing audiovisual work, limited unpaid resources and the need for independent teams to share responsibility.
articles.note: Pages 116–118 are an appended editorial response, distinguished here from the contributor’s argument. Dates, priority claims and descriptions of institutions are not independently certified by this gist.

articles.title: Maithili in the Digital Age: Videha and Gajendra Thakur
articles.author: Vikas Vatsnabh
articles.gist: Vatsnabh connects language survival online with usable scripts, Unicode, technical vocabulary and substantial searchable content. He treats Videha as a journal, library and resource aggregator, and discusses dictionaries and Panji publication as collaborative work. The closing argument looks toward AI: sustained digital availability, rather than symbolic recognition alone, is presented as essential infrastructure for Maithili.
articles.note: The contents spells the surname ‘Vatsanabh’; the article heading prints ‘Vatsnabh’.

articles.title: Gajendra Thakur’s Contribution to the Preservation of Mithila’s Panji
articles.author: Bhairav Lal Das
articles.gist: Das separates Panji’s value as a historical source from the hierarchy and misuse associated with its social administration. He credits the joint editors of the published records and recounts practical conservation efforts frustrated by mistrust, declining livelihoods and deteriorating manuscripts. He calls for further preservation and publication while considering how migration and changing marriage practices alter the records’ former function.

articles.title: Diversity and Videha: The Consciousness-Based Renaissance of Modern Maithili Literature
articles.author: Poonam Jha ‘Sudha’
articles.gist: Jha organizes her argument around linguistic, writerly and thematic diversity. She presents Videha’s acceptance of regional speech, younger voices and varied subjects as a challenge to narrow standards and centralized literary authority. Her account treats digital access as a bridge between rural and urban readers, generations and the diaspora, while discussing resistance to this openness as part of the debate.

articles.title: Diversity and Videha
articles.author: Dr. Shiv Kumar Prasad
articles.gist: Prasad supports his account of diversity with an extended survey of writers, publications and quoted examples. Discussions of Jagadish Prasad Mandal, Umesh Paswan, Rajdev Mandal, Bechan Thakur, Munni Kamat and others connect lived rural experience with poetry, fiction, drama and criticism. He sees the parallel literary stream as a change in who can speak and which experiences receive sustained attention.

articles.title: Videha and New Writers
articles.author: Kalpana Jha
articles.gist: Jha defines editing as mentorship rather than selection alone. Drawing on her own beginnings and the experiences of other writers, she describes encouragement, suggested reading, criticism and help with genre and craft. Her central demand is that guidance strengthen a writer’s distinct voice while building a new generation of contributors and connecting their abilities with readers’ expectations.

articles.title: Scarcity of Non-Forward Caste Writers in Maithili and Gajendra Thakur
articles.author: Munnaji
articles.gist: Munnaji disputes the claim that Maithili lacks writers from socially marginalized communities. He argues that publication opportunities and sustained encouragement make previously excluded talent visible, using Jagadish Prasad Mandal and later contributors as examples. The essay presents Videha’s significance as the creation of an enduring alternative stream; its account of literary gatekeeping is the contributor’s polemical interpretation.

articles.title: The Pro-People Stance of Videha Magazine
articles.author: Dr. Dhanakar Thakur
articles.gist: Thakur evaluates Videha through five areas: language, writers, subjects and genres, awards, and special issues. He values openness beyond a single ideology, while acknowledging uneven spelling and disagreeing with the naming of parallel awards. The resulting assessment is supportive but qualified: widening participation matters, yet a magazine’s public responsibility remains unfinished and open to criticism.

articles.title: Gajendra Thakur and the Discipline of Maithili Criticism
articles.author: Hitnath Jha
articles.gist: Jha reviews Maithili Samikshashastra as a guide to evaluating genres rather than praising personalities. He discusses distinctions between short narrative forms, the demands of ghazal metre, other poetic forms, translation and children’s literature. The review emphasizes judging craft and meaning without imposing the critic’s ideology, and presents the book as useful to writers, teachers, students and researchers.

articles.title: Gajendra Thakur: Writer, Historian, and Architect of Modern Maithili Studies
articles.author: Praveen Kumar Jha
articles.gist: Jha offers a biographical and bibliographical overview linking creative writing, Panji editing, lexicography, script work and digital publishing. He reads these activities as a connection between inherited scholarship and contemporary access. An appended editorial note clarifies institutional memberships and website work; the gist preserves the distinction between the contributor’s profile and editorial additions without treating biographical speculation as established fact.

articles.title: An Incomparable and Unique Contribution
articles.author: Kundan Karn
articles.gist: Karn recounts discovering Videha after a lockdown-era short narrative attracted Munnaji’s attention. His account centres on encouragement, approachable correspondence and the gradual discovery of Gajendra Thakur’s wider work. He explicitly acknowledges limited familiarity with the creative corpus and no personal meeting, making this a testimony about an emerging writer’s experience rather than a comprehensive literary assessment.

articles.title: Gajendra Thakur ji’s Contribution to Maithili Literature
articles.author: Jagadanand Jha ‘Manu’
articles.gist: Jha offers an appreciative survey of research, dictionaries, scripts, translation, literary forms and digital archives. He places particular emphasis on the editor’s ability to identify new talent and connect dispersed readers with books and periodicals. The essay’s large output totals and priority claims belong to its tribute-oriented account and are not adopted here as a reconciled bibliography.

articles.title: Gajendra Thakur: The Bridge-Person for the Renaissance of Maithili Language and Literature
articles.author: Ujjwal Kumar Jha
articles.gist: Jha uses bridge-building to connect Thakur’s writing, historical research, script preservation, dictionaries, translation and editorial work. He interprets literary creation as a cultural responsibility extending to young readers and future researchers. The essay’s organizing idea is continuity across tradition and technology, reinforced by an account of translation as exchange between Maithili, English and other Indian languages.

articles.title: Gajendra Thakur’s Absence from the Forums of Mithila–Maithili: Causes and Effects
articles.author: Mukesh Anand
articles.gist: Anand contrasts public-platform recognition with sustained work away from ceremonies, drawing on his experience of Delhi’s literary environment. He offers possible explanations for Videha’s limited institutional visibility and asks readers to judge contribution through study rather than invitations or awards. He also stresses collaborators’ roles and argues that distance from platforms may preserve time for substantive work.

articles.title: Contributor and editor introductions; closing invocation
articles.author: Editorial compilation; no separate byline
articles.gist: The final pages identify the sixteen contributors and briefly describe their literary or research activities, followed by an introduction to editor Ashish Anchinhaar. A closing invocation is addressed to readers. These are attribution and framing materials, not an additional signed critical essay; the descriptions reflect the supplied edition rather than independently updated biographies.
